artist: Sam Doores + Riley Downing & The Tumbleweeds
label: Self-released
description: An early record credited to Sam Doores and Riley Downing, who would go on to front The Deslondes, played in a ramshackle country-blues style they'd carry into that band. It leans on upright bass, loose acoustic guitars, and weathered group harmonies, closer to a porch session than a studio record. It's for anyone tracing the roots of the Deslondes' street-corner sound back before the band had its name.
lineage: Sam Doores and Riley Downing, both credited here, later co-founded The Deslondes; this is the pre-Deslondes form of their shared songwriting.
borderline_note: Pre-2014, so V6 only (not eligible for C-lane secondary).

label: New West Records
description: Doores' debut solo record moves away from the Deslondes' New Orleans R&B-and-country stew toward quieter, piano- and acoustic-led songwriting. Songs like 'Let It Roll' and 'Other Side of Town' keep his easy, conversational drawl but trade the full band's boogie for more intimate arrangements. It's for Deslondes fans curious what one member sounds like on his own.
lineage: A solo record from Deslondes co-founder Sam Doores, released on the band's label, New West.

label: New West Records
description: Downing's first solo album is a leaner, more straightforwardly honky-tonk record than his main band, built on twangy electric guitar, pedal steel, and plainspoken breakup songs. The title track and 'Coleman Rose' lean into a classic country shuffle. It's the record for listeners who want the Deslondes' rootsier, more countrified side isolated and pushed forward.
lineage: A solo record from Deslondes co-frontman Riley Downing, released on the band's label, New West.

label: New West Records
description: A stripped-back, road-worn Deslondes record built on the band's habit of trading lead vocals and songwriting among members. 'Hold on Liza' and 'Pour Another Round' keep the barroom piano and multi-voice harmonies that define the band's sound, with less studio polish than 'Hurry Home' or 'Ways & Means'. It's for longtime fans following the band's New Orleans country-and-R&B blend.
lineage: The Deslondes' fourth studio album, continuing the shared-songwriting band founded by Sam Doores and Riley Downing.
borderline_note: Not previously staged; adds to the Deslondes catalog already in the atlas.

label: Mashed Potato Records
description: A three-song demo session released on Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records, catching Casey Jane Reece-Kaigler and Camille Wind Weatherford's paired voices before they had a full band identity. The recordings are spare and rough-edged, built on close harmony over simple guitar backing. It's a curiosity for tracing the Lostines back to their earliest New Orleans sessions.
lineage: Released on Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records, placing the duo in the same New Orleans DIY-country circle as the Deslondes.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: The New Orleans duo's proper debut EP, built on the two singers' tightly stacked harmonies over spare guitar and rhythm section. Tracks like 'Faith In Love' and 'Who's Your Love' favor early rock-and-roll and girl-group phrasing filtered through a country-folk band. It's the entry point for the Lostines' pre-full-length sound.
lineage: Follows their 2016 demos on Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records; released on Nick Shoulders' Gar Hole Records, tying them to the same New Orleans DIY-country scene.

label: Gar Hole Records / Mashed Potato Records
description: A split EP pairing two songs from The Lostines with two from Nick Shoulders & the Okay Crawdad, released jointly by Gar Hole Records and Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records to mark their overlapping years coming up in New Orleans. The Lostines' side moves from the electric-guitar dancehall stomp of 'A Tear' to the string-and-keyboard hush of 'Last Night'. It documents the small-label, shared-scene connections around the New Orleans Americana underground.
lineage: A cross-label collaboration linking The Lostines' Mashed Potato Records roots to Nick Shoulders' Gar Hole Records, both offshoots of the same New Orleans DIY country scene.
borderline_note: Split EP credited to two acts; staged under The Lostines since this batch covers their catalog.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: The Lostines' full-length debut folds 1960s girl-group harmony singing into a New Orleans roots-band frame, with fiddle, pedal steel, and swooning strings behind Casey Jane Reece-Kaigler and Camille Wind Weatherford's tightly entwined voices. Songs like 'Neon Lights' and 'Full Moon Night' move between late-night dancehall pop and quieter, string-laced balladry. It's the best entry point to the duo's sound.
lineage: Follows EPs released on Mashed Potato Records and Gar Hole Records, both New Orleans DIY-country labels; the girl-group-meets-honky-tonk sound is indebted to '60s pop harmony groups.

label: Bloodshot Records
description: Winslow-King's second Bloodshot Records album blends New Orleans R&B, ragtime-inflected fingerpicking, and slide guitar into a warm, gospel-tinged roots-rock sound. It's brighter and more arranged than straight blues, built around his easy tenor. Good for listeners who want the city's brass-band and blues traditions filtered through a songwriter's frame.
lineage: Esther Rose sang and played in his band before her solo career; he also shares the early-2010s New Orleans roots scene with Hurray for the Riff Raff and The Deslondes.

album: I'm Glad Trouble Don't Last Always
label: Bloodshot Records
description: A follow-up to 'Everlasting Arms' built on slide-guitar blues, New Orleans rhythm, and concise, hook-forward songs, with a looser, more electric feel than its predecessor. 'Esther Please' shows its plainspoken, personal side. It suits listeners drawn to the city's blues-and-roots lineage more than pure country twang.
lineage: Continues Winslow-King's run on Bloodshot Records; sits geographically and stylistically near the New Orleans roots circle of the Deslondes and Hurray for the Riff Raff.

label: Self-released
description: A folk-songwriting record that mixes in the French, Cajun, and R&B threads of New Orleans. It's a quiet, singer-songwriter set built around acoustic guitar and a clear, unforced voice, closer to porch-folk than her later, more band-driven work. For listeners tracing New Orleans folk voices adjacent to the Riff Raff/Deslondes scene.
lineage: Sounds akin to the early-2010s New Orleans street-folk and traditional-jazz crossover scene around Hurray for the Riff Raff.
borderline_note: Some sources (Spotify metadata, Antigravity Magazine) date this LP to 2012; used artist's own official bio date of 2013.

label: Self-released
description: A river-titled set pairing Quintana's folk guitar and voice with jazz- and Cajun-inflected arrangements. It's more fleshed-out than her debut, with a full band supporting story-songs about place and water. Good for fans of literate, regionally rooted folk songwriting.
lineage: Sounds rooted in New Orleans folk and traditional jazz, near the city's Americana scene.

label: Self-released
description: A short, intimate EP of acoustic story-songs, smaller in scale than her full-lengths but continuing the plainspoken folk style of her earlier records. It functions as a between-albums release rather than a major statement. Best for listeners already following her catalog.
lineage: A small release between 'Miss River' and her later, more produced work.

label: Self-released
description: Fronted by a full electric band, this album leans harder into vintage New Orleans R&B and Cajun two-step rhythms than her earlier folk-leaning records. It's a looser, more rhythmic record built for dancing, with the rolling piano-and-horns feel of the city's '50s and '60s R&B. Good for listeners who want Quintana's most fully arranged, band-forward work.
lineage: Sounds indebted to vintage New Orleans R&B in the Fats Domino/Irma Thomas vein, plus Cajun dance music.

album: That's All There Is (And There Ain't No More)
label: Muddy Roots Records
description: A hard-country record steeped in honky-tonk shuffles and blue-collar songwriting, with Reedy's plainspoken voice out front. It's twangier and more traditionalist than the Deslondes' genre-blending, closer to classic Bakersfield/outlaw phrasing than to R&B. For listeners who want working-class honky-tonk played straight.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Bakersfield and outlaw country; kin in spirit to the New Orleans street-country of the Deslondes.

label: Self-released
description: A record built around travel and homesickness, keeping the band's classic honky-tonk instrumentation of twangy electric guitar and pedal steel under Reedy's plainspoken, working-class songwriting. It's a more settled record than the band's earlier, rowdier output. For fans of traditionalist country songwriting with a road-worn edge.
lineage: Sounds indebted to classic honky-tonk and outlaw country, continuing the sound of 'That's All There Is (And There Ain't No More)'.
borderline_note: Reedy now based in Chicago; scene tag kept as New Orleans since the band formed and is rooted there.

album: The Place That You Call Home
label: Parish Road Music
description: The debut album by New Orleans songwriter Kelcy Mae Wilburn under the band name Ever More Nest, an Americana record centered on place and rootedness. It pairs a plainspoken, weathered alto with pedal steel and understated full-band arrangements, closer to alt-country balladry than to the city's brass-and-R&B side. It's for listeners who like quiet, place-rooted Americana songwriting.
lineage: Sounds akin to the 2010s New Orleans Americana scene around Hurray for the Riff Raff and The Deslondes.

label: Bayou Perdu Records
description: A Cajun record that runs traditional two-step fiddle and French-language singing through distortion pedals and rock-band volume, closer to a noisy roots-punk gig than a dancehall set. It's trad-Cajun instrumentation (fiddle, accordion) pushed into feedback and fuzz. It's for listeners exploring how far a traditional Louisiana form can be pushed toward rock.
lineage: Sits in the trad-Cajun/newgrass Context lane rather than the Deslondes/Riff Raff alt-country lineage, but shares the same New Orleans-area roots-music community and stages; the split is genre (trad Cajun vs. country-rock songwriting) rather than geography.
borderline_note: Placed in X4 (Cajun/trad) rather than V6 per assignment; included for scene context only.

label: Rice Pump Records
description: A Grammy-winning Cajun record that folds synthesizers and studio effects into traditional fiddle-and-accordion two-steps, continuing the band's project of modernizing Cajun music without abandoning its French-language core. It's denser and more electronic than 'Mammoth Waltz', while keeping the same two-step dance rhythms. For listeners wanting the trad-Cajun wing of the wider Louisiana roots scene.
lineage: Same trad-Cajun lineage as 'Mammoth Waltz'; connected to the broader New Orleans-area Americana community by geography and shared festival stages, not by songwriting style.
borderline_note: Placed in X4 (Cajun/trad) rather than V6 per assignment; included for scene context only.
